summary: Defines a link-type sub-TLV for OSPF and IS-IS that tells how many traffic engineering label switched paths with zero reserved bandwidth cross a link. Using this count, a path computation can make better statistical guesses about the real load on a link. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Some cars reserve no seats but still ride the bus. This lets a router report how many of these unreserved riders are on each road, so planners get a better idea of how crowded it is.

questions: number of zero bandwidth te lsps
ospf is-is sub-tlv unreserved lsp count
what is an unconstrained te lsp
how does is-is advertise zero bandwidth te lsps
subtitle: A new OSPF and IS-IS sub-TLV that reports how many zero-bandwidth traffic engineering tunnels cross a link.

tldr.problem: Traffic engineering tunnels signalled with zero bandwidth reserve nothing, so routers cannot tell how many of them share a link, and equal cost paths cannot be balanced well.
tldr.mechanism: A new optional sub-TLV, type 23, carries the number of such tunnels crossing a link in OSPF (inside the Link TLV) and in IS-IS (inside TLV 22 or TLV 222).
tldr.outcome: Path computations can use the count to make statistical load-balancing choices, though the RFC leaves the algorithms themselves out of scope. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5330 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Zero-Bandwidth Tunnel Problem
sections.content:
Operators sometimes deploy MPLS Traffic Engineering just for fast recovery, using MPLS TE Fast Reroute (RFC 4090). A common model is a full mesh of TE LSPs signalled with zero bandwidth between a set of label switching routers, each protected by pre-established backup tunnels. The RFC calls these unconstrained TE LSPs. Their traffic simply follows the IGP shortest path, because the computed path is no different from it when the TE metric equals the IGP metric.

The trouble shows up when a tunnel is reoptimized. Path cost and hop count may not help, for example in a symmetrical network with equal cost multi-paths (ECMP). Several equal cost paths can exist, and since the tunnels reserve nothing, the reservable bandwidth along each path cannot break the tie. The result can be poorly balanced traffic.
sections.eli5: If lots of cars take the same road but none of them book a spot, a planner looking at the booking list sees every road as empty and cannot pick the least busy one.

sections.title: Counting Instead of Reserving
sections.content:
The idea is that, by making statistical assumptions about the aggregated traffic of a set of unconstrained TE LSPs, algorithms can be designed to load balance existing or new tunnels across equal cost paths. That needs one piece of knowledge: how many unconstrained TE LSPs are signalled across each link.

The existing link sub-TLVs for OSPF and IS-IS (RFC 3630 and RFC 5305) advertise things like available bandwidth, TE metric and administrative group, but not this count. The RFC specifies only the new piece of advertised information. The load balancing algorithms are explicitly outside its scope and are mentioned only to explain the motivation. The count could also be used for other purposes, such as estimating how many unconstrained tunnels a link failure would affect.

Unconstrained TE LSPs configured and provisioned through a management system MAY be left out of the reported count.
sections.eli5: Since nobody books seats, the router instead counts heads. A head count per road is enough for a planner to guess which road is busiest.

sections.title: The Unconstrained TE LSP Count Sub-TLV
sections.content:
Two versions are defined, both with type value 23. Each is OPTIONAL and MUST NOT appear more than once in its parent. If a second instance is present, the receiver MUST process only the first.

In IS-IS, the sub-TLV sits inside the extended IS reachability TLV (type 22, from RFC 5305) or the Multi-Topology Intermediate Systems TLV (type 222, from RFC 5120). It has a 1-octet type of 23, a 1-octet length of 2 and a 2-octet value holding the number of unconstrained TE LSPs signalled across the link.

In OSPF, the sub-TLV sits inside the Link TLV (type 2), which is carried in the Traffic Engineering LSA from RFC 3630 or in the OSPFv3 Intra-Area-TE LSA (function code 10) from RFC 5329. It has a 2-octet type of 23, a 2-octet length of 4 and a 4-octet value with the count.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny labeled box on the road report that holds one number, the count of unreserved riders. IS-IS uses a smaller box and OSPF a bigger one.

sections.title: Elements of Procedure
sections.content:
If the sub-TLV is absent, that SHOULD be read as an absence of information about the link, not as a count of zero.

As with other MPLS TE link characteristics, the rules for when a router originates a new LSA or LSP are outside the scope of this document. The RFC adds a caution: care must be taken not to trigger systematic flooding of a new IS-IS LSP or OSPF LSA at too fine a granularity whenever the number of unconstrained TE LSPs changes.
sections.eli5: If a road report has no head count, it does not mean the road is empty, it just means nobody counted. Also, do not send a fresh report every time one rider hops on.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA defined a sub-registry for the sub-TLVs carried in IS-IS TLV 22 and assigned the new codepoint 23 to the Unconstrained TE LSP Count sub-TLV there. It also defined a sub-registry for the sub-TLVs carried in the OSPF TE Link TLV (type 2) and assigned the value 23 for the same sub-TLV. Both entries reference RFC 5330.
sections.eli5: The number 23 was written in the official list so everyone uses the same label for this box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the function it describes creates no new security issues for OSPF and IS-IS. It points to RFC 2328 and RFC 5340 for the base OSPF security considerations, and to RFC 1195 and RFC 5304 for IS-IS. A security framework for MPLS and GMPLS is cited as a work in progress.
sections.eli5: Adding one more number to the report does not make it any easier to cheat, so the old safety rules still apply.
